chapter_theme: Test a friend before taking him: by learning, by family, by loyalty under injury, by constancy, and by whether he actually helps. The reason is given at the end: once a bond is formed, parting hurts even when the friend was a snake.
structure_note: 211 to 216 sort friends through images (sugarcane eaten from either end, elephant and dog, tree flowers and pond flowers, three kinds of palm). 217 to 219 weigh what a friend's love, help and understanding are worth. 220 gives the reason for all the testing.

211.reading: Friendship with those who have learned with understanding is always like eating sugarcane from the tip down, sweeter as one goes; the bond with those who lack sweetness is like eating it from the root toward the tip.
211.nuance: The quatrain nearly repeats 138 in the chapter on learning, with a different refrain. Mudaliar explains that eating from the tip makes the cane grow sweeter as one goes, and from the root less sweet.

positions.position: The sweetness the second group lacks is the sweetness of learning.
positions.quote: கல்வியறி வாகிய இனிய தன்மை யில்லாதவர்களது நட்பு

positions.position: The sweetness they lack is a sweet disposition, as Pope also has it.

212.reading: Lord of the flowering hills, where birds scatter as golden water pours down, one may befriend people on the good ground that, mindful of their family, they will not change midway; apart from that, a person's mind is not something that can be known.
212.nuance: The verse doesn't praise high birth for its own sake. It falls back on lineage because the mind can't be read. Mudaliar draws the rule: befriend those of high family.

213.reading: Give up the friendship of those who are like elephants and hold close those who are like dogs: the elephant may kill even its keeper after knowing him for years, while the dog wags its tail with its master's spear in its body.
213.nuance: The test is loyalty under injury, not strength or rank: the elephant is the nobler animal and still loses.

214.reading: Those who are not joined in heart for even a few days do not become close, though they stay beside one for many days; and would anyone let go of the bond with those tied to their heart because they have been away for many days?
214.nuance: Nearness and distance are both set aside: the heart's tie alone makes and keeps a friend. Shanmuganar supplies 'the great' as the subject.

215.reading: The true conduct of friendship is to go on loving what it first loved, like a tree's flower that opens and doesn't close again; no one esteems or befriends those who open first and close later, like the flowers of a dug pond.
215.nuance: Pond flowers such as the lotus close each evening, so the fault condemned is changeability, not coldness.

216.reading: In friendship the lowest are like the areca palm and the middle like the coconut; the bond of the highest, who keep old ties, is like the palmyra of untold worth: what was given on the first day stays given.
216.nuance: Mudaliar explains the trees: the areca yields only with constant tending, the coconut with occasional tending, and the palmyra gives richly after a single watering. On that reading the grades measure how much a friend has to be given before the friendship yields.

217.reading: Even dark greens cooked in rice-water are ambrosia if someone gives them with high regard; white rice with fine seasonings and relishes, taken from the hand of those not in accord with one, is the bitter strychnos fruit.

218.reading: What use is the friendship of those as close as the little toe on a dog's foot who give not even a fly's foot of help? Go even far to gain the bond of those who are like the channel that makes the field yield.
218.nuance: Nearness is set against usefulness, and the channel image implies that real help often comes from a distance.

219.reading: Enmity is better than the friendship of those without clear understanding, death better than an incurable disease, killing kinder than contempt that wounds, and abuse better than praise of qualities one doesn't have.
219.nuance: Only the first of the four comparisons concerns friendship; the other three give it company. Mudaliar's gloss of கோறல் is printed as 'சொல்லுதல்' (speaking), probably an error for கொல்லுதல் (killing), which Shanmuganar and Pope have.

220.reading: Mix with many over many days, find who matches you, and take only those worth valuing; for it is painful to part after becoming close, even with a snake whose quick bite kills.
220.nuance: The argument rests on the cost of parting: because breaking a bond hurts even when the friend was deadly, the testing must come first.

links.note: A near doublet: both compare friendship with the learned to eating sugarcane from the tip and the other kind to eating it from the root. 138 ends on those without character or kindness, 211 on those without sweetness.
Both say friendship with the right people grows sweeter with use. 783 compares it to a book whose delight grows with study; 211 to sugarcane eaten from the tip.

212 relies on family as the only workable guarantee that a friend won't change, since minds can't be known. 245 says people are not like their இனம் but like their minds. The tension holds if 245's இனம் includes family, as Mudaliar's 'இனத்தார்' allows; if it means only the company one keeps, the two are about different things.
793 tells one to know a man's qualities, family, faults and connections before befriending him. 212 keeps family but doubts the rest: the mind can't be known, so family is the one dependable ground.

Both prize love that survives injury from the friend: 807 says those bound by love don't stop loving even when the friend ruins them, and 213 pictures the dog wagging its tail with the spear in its body.
Both say that a shared heart, not meeting or long acquaintance, makes friendship. 214 adds the reverse case: long absence doesn't break it.
Both use a flower's opening and closing for inconstant friendship. 425 says understanding is not opening and closing; 215 contrasts tree flowers that stay open with pond flowers that close.
104 says those who know its value count a millet-sized help as palmyra-sized. On Mudaliar's reading the palmyra in 216 stands for the best friends, who form a great friendship from one small help.

Both prefer hostility from the right people to friendship with the wrong. 187 says the enmity of the wise brings dignity; 219 says enmity is better than the friendship of those without clear understanding.
816 says being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool. 219 goes further: open enmity is better than a fool's friendship.
Both argue for testing before befriending because a formed bond can't be cleanly undone. 791 gives the reason as the friend's own loyalty; 220 gives it as the pain of parting, even from a snake.
Both say parting from a bad bond still hurts. 168 concludes that it is best to mix with no one; 220 concludes that one must test long before mixing.

source_issues: 213 and 220: the Tamil has corrupted characters (நண்பெரிணஇ for நண்பொரீஇ; மாணஇ, பெரிணஇ, பாணஇ, மாணஇஇ in 220 where Mudaliar's glosses have மரீஇ, பொரீஇ, பரீஇ).
219: Mudaliar's gloss reads 'கோறல் -சொல்லுதல்', probably a misprint for கொல்லுதல்.
220: Pope's translation has only a title; the text is a separator line. The shanmuganar field ends with the header of chapter 23.
